title: Kareena and Prithviraj, Both in Khaki, Finally Share a Frame. Meghna Gulzar's Daayra Locks Ganesh Chaturthi.
excerpt: A song-less crime thriller, two cops on opposite sides of a line, and the Raazi director pulling the strings. September 18 just became unmissable.
body:
Some pairings you wait years for without realizing you were waiting. **Kareena Kapoor Khan** in khaki. **Prithviraj Sukumaran** across from her, jaw set, eyes doing the talking. A serpent of tension coiling between two cops who may not be on the same side of the line they've both sworn to hold. On June 18, the makers of **Daayra** locked September 18, 2026 — Ganesh Chaturthi weekend — and dropped a behind-the-scenes glimpse that landed like a dare. "Some lines are drawn. Some lines are crossed. A choice awaits," reads the tagline. Consider us seated.

This is, somehow, the first time these two have shared a frame. Kareena, 45 and still the most magnetic presence in any room she walks into, hasn't been on screen since *Singham Again* in 2024. Prithviraj — the Malayalam superstar who directs, produces, and acts with the same restless intensity — last did Hindi with *Sarzameen*. Putting them opposite each other, both in police uniform, both "courageous, strong, and intense," as the set footage tells it, is the kind of casting coup that makes trade analysts sit up. Junglee Pictures' Amrita Pandey called it exactly that: a pairing that "elevates the film to another level."

> "KAREENA KAPOOR KHAN — PRITHVIRAJ SUKUMARAN: 'DAAYRA' RELEASE DATE LOCKED. Exactly 3 months from today." — Taran Adarsh

And then there's the woman behind the camera, who may be the real headline here. **Meghna Gulzar** doesn't make noise; she makes *Raazi*. She makes *Talvar*. She makes films that crawl under your skin and stay there, built on moral ambiguity and the quiet devastation of ordinary people caught in impossible systems. *Daayra* marks her third collaboration with Junglee Pictures, and it's billed as an intense crime-drama thriller — inspired by true events — that "explores the age-old paradox of crime, punishment, and justice." In Gulzar's hands, that logline isn't marketing fluff. It's a promise that nobody walks out clean.

Here's the detail that tells you what kind of film this is: **Daayra has no songs.** None. Back in February, lyricist-filmmaker Gulzar (Meghna's father) revealed that Meghna told him her script simply didn't allow for any. In an industry where the item number and the romantic duet are practically structural load-bearing walls, a song-less Hindi thriller is a statement of confidence. It says: the tension is the soundtrack. The silence is the score.

The behind-the-scenes glimpse Kareena posted leaned hard into that mood — raw, unpolished, both leads in uniform, no glamour, no gloss. "This one is for the books," she wrote. "Raw and unseen." It's a deliberate pivot from the high-shine star image she's cultivated for two decades, and it works. There's something thrilling about watching an actor of her wattage strip it all back and trust the material.

**For the diaspora, the timing is delicious.** September 18 falls right around Ganesh Chaturthi, one of the biggest festival windows for NRI audiences in the US, UK, and Canada, when families head to the cinema together and overseas box office spikes. Junglee Pictures and Pen Studios, with Pen Marudhar handling distribution, will almost certainly push a wide international theatrical release — expect screens in New Jersey, the Bay Area, London's Harrow and Wembley, and the Toronto-Brampton corridor. A Meghna Gulzar thriller with two powerhouse leads is exactly the kind of mid-budget, high-prestige title that travels well to diaspora multiplexes, where audiences increasingly hunger for substance over spectacle.

What makes *Daayra* especially intriguing is the cultural collision baked into the casting itself. Kareena is Bollywood royalty, fourth-generation Kapoor, the embodiment of Hindi-film glamour. Prithviraj is the thinking person's South superstar, beloved across Kerala for choosing brains over box-office formula. Watching their two distinct screen languages — her instinctive star charisma, his coiled, technical precision — collide inside a Meghna Gulzar moral maze is the genuine appeal here. Pan-Indian cinema keeps promising these North-South fusions; few arrive with this much pedigree attached.

There's no trailer yet, and that's smart. Let the curiosity build. Right now all we have is a tagline, a release date, and two actors in uniform staring down something we can't see. But if *Daayra* delivers on even half of what *Raazi* and *Talvar* did, September 18 won't be a release — it'll be an event. Mark it. The dream team is assembling, and for once, the hype feels earned.
